articles.text: Editor: I have been a resident of Piedmont a good part of my life. My family moved here in 1953. I attended Piedmont schools and left after I graduated from Piedmont High in 1969 to pursue my education and life and did not return until 1994. However, my parents remained, and so I witnessed the demolition of the high school, which was architecturally beautiful with spacious and light-filled classrooms. It was razed because of what turned out to be an unfounded concern that the structure was not earthquake sound. It was replaced by a structure that has since been replaced because it was seismically unsound. I saw the loss of Hamby’s, the drug store, and the Sweet Shoppe (in the middle of town) when the site was “improved” in the early 1970s and is now occupied by Wells Fargo and offices. I saw Safeway, which had a butcher, exit to be replaced by a bank and Convenient, now fortunately Mulberry’s. The latest plan to address the state’s housing mandate, to raze the Veterans Hall, relocate the police and fire department and additionally build on the tennis courts and the grassy strip on Highland, is even more poorly conceived and is distressing. The proposed changes to the city’s core would be a travesty and would forever change the character of Piedmont. While understanding the need to respond to the legislature’s mandate, the community would be ill-served by these proposals. Moving the fire department to the outskirts of the city would be a detriment to public safety. Has anyone considered the impact of rush hour gridlock on Moraga Avenue would have on the ability of emergency responders to get into the heart of the city when there is an urgent need? Objections to the proposal to build in Blair Park and the complaint that the residents of this housing would be “isolated” ignore the even more remote locations of residences on Maxwelton Road, Abbott Way, Echo Lane, and Nellie Avenue. Rezoning on Grand Avenue to accommodate multi-family housing is logical. The infrastructure already exists, and it would be situated on the only existing street in the city that could accommodate the additional traffic if restored to four lanes. The proposal to alter the city center, which has the endorsement of individuals who are not city residents, specifically staff and the outside consultants, is insensitive and out of touch with the community. Moving the tennis courts away from [proximity to] the high school would be a detriment to the school and raise its own safety issues. We are not Woodside, whose residents are seeking to avoid the construction of housing by prioritizing the needs of mountain lions. Our 1.7 square miles of land is already developed. articles.text: Editor: The time has come for Piedmont residents concerned about locating 215 or so low-income housing units to propose, rather than reject, sites. Proposals should, I believe, avoid assigning all, or nearly all, the units to one location. Fifty years of research tells us that day-to-day problems encountered by all communities, regardless of income distribution or history, become more divisive and difficult to solve in cities that create, by policy, low-income, stigmatized enclaves. And although the architectural community may believe otherwise, experience tells us that design alone will not overcome the stigma problem. The stig ma associated with concentrated, low-income enclaves has led to other approaches including “voucher” programs that enable low-income families to participate in the rental market. This approach will not work in the Bay Area because the supply of affordable housing remains so limited that vouchers simply lead to inflated rents. The “next-best” alternative has been “scattered site housing” or affordable units broadly distributed, in small groupings, in a community. Research finds that this approach creates less stigma and leads to better integration of families into the schools and social life of a community than do larger, concentrated enclaves. I suggest that Piedmont pursue, consistent with adopted city policy, the scattered site strategy. I propose a “5 by 40” approach meaning we should find 5 sites where 40 units can be reasonably integrated into the city. I recommend 40 units because research suggests that the relationship between project size and stigma is not linear. After about 40 units, the stigma accelerates quickly. I nominate 5 sites: • the corporation yard (yes, my “backyard”) • the skateboard park near the corporation yard • the Sylvan Learning Center and Ace Hardware sites on Grand Avenue • the land occupied by Highland Way • the last 15 units could go on the site city staff has identified on Park Boulevard The only “new” site here is Highland Way. The city owns the land. Using it for housing would not require replacing an existing city facility. All utilities and infrastructure are on site. Adjacent uses are commercial and institutional with height and mass consistent with multi-unit housing. Keeping 20 yards or so at the western terminus as a street would, moreover, preserve access for the gas station and pedestrian steps to the church. I look forward to seeing other schemes for a 5 by 40 solution.

Proposals should, I believe, avoid assigning all, or nearly all, the units to one location. Fifty years of research tells us that day-to-day problems encountered by all communities, regardless of income distribution or history, become more divisive and difficult to solve in cities that create, by policy, low-income, stigmatized enclaves. And although the architectural community may believe otherwise, experience tells us that design alone will not overcome the stigma problem. The stig ma associated with concentrated, low-income enclaves has led to other approaches including “voucher” programs that enable low-income families to participate in the rental market. This approach will not work in the Bay Area because the supply of affordable housing remains so limited that vouchers simply lead to inflated rents. The “next-best” alternative has been “scattered site housing” or affordable units broadly distributed, in small groupings, in a community. Research finds that this approach creates less stigma and leads to better integration of families into the schools and social life of a community than do larger, concentrated enclaves. I suggest that Piedmont pursue, consistent with adopted city policy, the scattered site strategy. I propose a “5 by 40” approach meaning we should find 5 sites where 40 units can be reasonably integrated into the city. I recommend 40 units because research suggests that the relationship between project size and stigma is not linear. After about 40 units, the stigma accelerates quickly. I nominate 5 sites: • the corporation yard (yes, my “backyard”) • the skateboard park near the corporation yard • the Sylvan Learning Center and Ace Hardware sites on Grand Avenue • the land occupied by Highland Way • the last 15 units could go on the site city staff has identified on Park Boulevard The only “new” site here is Highland Way. The city owns the land. Using it for housing would not require replacing an existing city facility. All utilities and infrastructure are on site. Adjacent uses are commercial and institutional with height and mass consistent with multi-unit housing. Keeping 20 yards or so at the western terminus as a street would, moreover, preserve access for the gas station and pedestrian steps to the church. articles.text: On July 28, the Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD) reported over 750 confirmed monkeypox cases in California, 58 of which are Alameda County residents. Monkeypox is a disease belonging to the Orthpoxvirus genus, which includes smallpox, and is caused by a pathogen or infectious agent that has jumped from an animal host to human. Monkeypox occurs naturally in Africa, and is described by the County Health office as “a disease… that has been rarely exported to other regions beyond Central and West Africa.” Symptoms of monkeypox include flu-like illness, fever, headache, swollen lymph nodes, chills and fatigue. These symptoms are followed by a rash that typically begins on the face or hands. Lesions are well-rounded and resemble pimples; scabs are described by patients as painful until the healing phase when they become itchy and crust. “Any rash-like illness consistent with the clinical descriptions above during travel or upon return should be immediately reported to a health care professional, including information about all recent travel, sexual history, and smallpox immunization history,” said Dr. Nicolas Moss, Alameda County Public Health Officer. Monkeypox can spread through touching materials used by an infected person that haven’t been cleaned, such as clothing, towels and bedding. It can also spread by respiratory secretions during prolonged, close, faceto-face contact, according to the Center for Disease Control (CDC). The County has created a screening worksheet and urges all individuals with symptoms of Monkeypox to complete the worksheet, which requires the patient to send photos of rashes and collect specimens. The form is available at https://acphd-web-media.s3-uswest-2.amazonaws.com/media/ communicable-disease/monkeypox/docs/monkeypox-screening-form-2022.07.10.pdf. Questions may be directed to the County Health office by e-mail at monkeypox@acgov.org, or by calling 510-267-3250. Individuals experiencing symptoms may also call an on-call ACPHD Public Health Duty Officer at (925) 422-7595. State response The California Department of Public Health is monitoring monkeypox transmission in the state and throughout the U.S. “The risk of monkeypox to the public is currently very low based on the information available. While monkeypox can infect anyone, many of the recent cases in 2022 have occurred among persons self-identifying as men who have sex with men,” said CDPH Director Dr. Tomas Aragon. “Vaccination helps to protect against monkeypox when given before or shortly after an exposure. JYNNEOS and ACAM2000 are two monkeypox vaccines currently available in the United States via the Strategic National Stockpile.” As of August 1, the federal government has allocated a limited number of JYNNEOS vaccine doses to Californians. “CDPH is working with local health departments to make these doses available to protect against monkeypox,” Dr. Aragon confirmed. The state department recommends avoiding close physical contact with people who have symptoms, wear personal protective equipment including masks, and to practice good hand hygiene. articles.text: As the calendar inches its way through the summer into fall, today marks one week before Piedmont students return to school, August 10. Whether summer has entered the dog days or flown by, starting a creative project is rewarding for everyone. Creating a zine can be that be end-of-summer fun project. A zine is a homemade production of a magazine on a small scale. A zine may be nothing more than a flip book, or a single sheet of paper that is folded into a small 8-page pamphlet. Zines have grown in popularity and possess a counter-culture of “rebellion” as media in a physical form with anonymity. However, the creation of a zine can quietly work the brain and improve scholastic skills while having fun. Potential topics are endless for your kid’s’ creative project. It can be a how-to booklet, a joke book, a superhero comic book, or just a collection of photos. Simply folding and cutting the paper and mapping out the page numbers can be enough of a spark to have kids feeling like the next renegade anonymous artist with the fame of Banksy awaiting them. As digital media dominates the life of kids (and adults) via online school and work, parents The one page mini-zine is created with a couple of folds, a cut in the middle of the paper pages numbered as shown. may be looking for anything in the physical realm to ease the strain on their kids’ eyes. Even if your child does not have the gift of writing or drawing, they can have fun making a zine which can expand their horizons beyond a screen. Consider diving into multi-media by cutting out pictures from old magazines or newspaper; that can be done by anyone with or without any artistic ability. One doesn’t need a story to tell to create a zine; it doesn’t have to make any sense. Once the work of art is completed, the process of distribution can be the most fun of all. After making photocopies, your kids can give them out to friends, patrons at Mulberry’s Market, or neighbors. They can be anonymously inside books at a bookstore or library. Leaving one’s creation in public, even at the tiny free libraries, means there’s no limit to the places they will end up. The sand of summer’s hourglass may be dwindling, but there is still time for one last fun amazine project.

articles.text: School is coming. Having the kids out of the house will be nice, but we need to make sure they are ready to go when they get back to school. So, the questions are, “Should we prep for school or just rest? When do we start? How hard do we push? Where do we go for help? Do we review or learn new material?” Let’s address each one individually. To Prep or Not to Prep To answer this question, we need to assess the students’ circumstances and the students themselves. If your student is going to enter their freshman year, they will most likely spend a good portion of the beginning of the year with preparatory instruction since none of the freshman will know what high school is like. If your student is going into the junior year or is in middle school, and their grades are on the fence, you probably don’t have the leeway of a slow start and should get your student ready to hit the ground running. When Should You Start? Once you have decided that you need to get your student ready for school ahead of time, the next question is when should you start. Some parents decide not to take a break at all. For students who struggle or tend to lose a lot of ground during the summer, this makes sense. For other students who want to be ready for a solid start, a few weeks or just a week of prep is generally enough since most students will have some review at the start of the year and just need to make sure their school brain is in gear. What to Study? You can review the material from last year or front load the new material. If you are studyIt is a good idea to do some academic preparation before school begins. ing math or foreign languages, it makes the most sense to review the material from last year since the classes are likely cumulative. If you are getting ready for any other class that is not cumulative, review the material that the class will cover at the start of the year. If you hire a tutoring service or an ex-teacher, a lot of the leg work on finding what to learn will be done for you. Otherwise, you can get a lot of information and help at the California standards website (www.cde.ca.gov/ be/st/ss/), or contact us for more information. Who Should Teach the Material? For motivated students, all you will need to do is point them in the right direction and let them go. Other students will need a parent or tutor to set up their prep work and gather their materials for them. It can be really hard for students to be motivated as summer comes to an end, so if you only have a few weeks to get ready, it probably makes sense not to rely solely on students without some supervision. What if It’s Too Late? It’s never too late, but it may be too late to get ready ahead of time in the summer. If you find the school year is upon you and your student isn’t ready, doing an extra review and studying at the start of the year can be almost as effective as summer pre-studying. Use the first few weeks to make sure any required knowledge is fresh and that students are familiar with the material that is coming. If you have any questions about prepping for the school year or any other education-related questions, please do not hesitate to contact Paul Osborne (DBA Paul the Tutor) at 4235 Piedmont Avenue. articles.text: Photos courtesy of International Fencing Federation Rafaella Gomes of Piedmont competed at the Fencing World Championship in Cairo, Egypt, reaching the Round of 64. Representing Brazil, Piedmont High School Class of 2021 graduate Rafaella Gomes recently competed on the world stage in the Fencing World Championship in Cairo, Egypt the week of July 15. Given the No. 46 overall seed in the preliminary round, she upset No. 19 Kim Kirschen of Germany 15-7. She attained the No. 61 seed in the Round of 64 and battled against the eventual runner up in the finals, No. 4 Arianna Errigo of Italy, losing 15-8. Her results improved Gomes’ world ranking from No. 100 to No. 77. “To make it to the second day is to compete with the greats. And I did just that, facing Arianna Errigo right off the bat. She is an amazing fencer, who I greatly respect and admire. I fenced the match with all I had, fueled partly by a newcomer’s burning desire to prove myself. Though I lost, I am proud of the way I fenced,” said Gomes. Facing Errigo is no easy task; the Italian eventually reached the Finals, where she lost to Ysoara Thibus of France 15-10. To take eight points from a finalist says a lot about Gomes’ potential. “The experience added fuel to my passion and to my ambition. I want to reach higher, and I am not afraid of the work it will take to make that happen,” she added. Prior to the tournament, Gomes had just two weeks to train for the tournament after recovering from COVID-19. She trains at the Massialas Foundation in San Francisco, a pre-Olympic program that Gomes trained with Rafaella Gomes (right) improved her world ranking in fencing to No. 77. articles.text: In its first time starting in Denmark, this year’s Tour de France winner was a Dane. Jonas Vingegaard, 25, officially dethroned Slovenia’s Tadej Pogačar for the Yellow Jersey on July 24, holding the lead in General Classification over the last 10 stages of Le Grand Boucle and finishing with a 2-minute, 43-second advantage. Vingegaard stunned the world on Stage 11 when overtaking Pogačar and building a staggering advantage when attacking on the Col du Granon with 3.5 kilometers to go. The Dane’s triumphant performance is a testament to the strength of his teammates on Jumbo-Visma, while Pogačar had little help from UAE Team Emirates. Jumbo-Visma continually attacked on Stage 11 to string Pogačar thin without necessary teammates to maintain a manageable pace. By the time the course reached Col du Granon, Vingegaard turned on the after-burners and cranked his way up the mountain, leaving Pogačar in the dust. Jumbo-Visma cyclist Wout Van Aert won the Green Jersey for the lead in Points Classification. Following Stage 11, Vingegaard prevented numerous attacks by Pogačar, including continuous sprints by the Slovenian on the mountains of stages 17 and 18. Pogačar was able to win Stage 17, but did so without picking up any time advantage on Vingegaard. The Jumbo-Visma rider, meanwhile won Stage 18 with a mighty 1 minute, 4 second advantage over Pogačar, solidifying his place as the next Tour de France champion. Questions loomed about whether the Slovenian used too much energy in the early portion of the tour, which seemed to be the case once Pogačar cracked on Stage 11. It prevented Pogačar from becoming the first three-time champion since Chris Froome in 2015-2017. Pogačar did win his third consecutive Best Young Rider classification. Vingegaard, meanwhile, was also crowned Best Climber. The 2023 Tour de France starting location has already been announced. articles.text: TRINITY ZAMORA Basketball Trinity Zamora was named honorable mention for the Post’s Athlete of the Year award after being named the WACC’s Player of the Year last season and a firstteam All-League recipient. She was named Sophomore of the Year in 2021 and Freshman of the Year in 2020 by the Post. Zamora helped lead the basketball team last winter to a 24-7 overall record. The team was runner-up in the North Coast Section, and advanced to the second round of the CIF State tournament as the No. 1 seed. It was the team’s first appearance in the NCS finals in 11 years. Zamora was the team’s leading rebounder, defender, and always a premier scoring presence. Some of Zamora’s highest outputs included 29 points in the NCS Finals, 23 points and 19 rebounds against Oakland Tech, and 28 points and 16 rebounds against Alameda. In two games with O’Dowd, she had 18 points and 22 rebounds and 17 points and 10 boards. MICHAEL AIKAWA Baseball Michael Aikawa emerged as a leader of the baseball team as a sophomore in 2021 and earned the Post’s Sophomore of the Year award this year. Staff Photos Michael Aikawa was the Post’s Sophomore of the Year. He enters his senior year as a key member of the baseball team. He’s competing this summer on a travel and participating in highlevel tournaments prior to the start of school this fall. He helped the Highlanders post a 19-9 record and a league title in the Shoreline Division. He earned a first-team All-League selection in the process. In 2022, Aikawa finished tied for the team lead with 29 hits and 25 runs scored, including four doubles, one triple, one home run, seven RBIs, and a batting average of .363. At State Parks, staff are conserving water by continually locating and repairing water leaks throughout their distribution systems, installing timers on irrigation systems, and implementing other water conservation efforts,” the park stated in a press release. The park is contacting impacted reservations to provide refunds. This comes with fire season waging in Northern California, predominantly with the ongoing McKinney Fire in the Klamath National Forest and Oak Fire waging in Mariposa County. Photo courtesy of CAStateParks.gov California State Parks declared that Peters Creek has a low amount of water flow, which requires them to shut down camping facilities. Portola Redwoods State Park is 2,800 acres large and offers 18 miles worth of hiking trails, 55 family campground sites, four group sites, a visitor center, and a trail camp for backpackers which is along the way to Peters Creek– which has an ancient grove of trees. Located in the South Bay, the park is frequently visited by Bay Area residents for a quick getaway to see some historic redwood trees and is usually fully booked long before the start of the summer months. We visited Portola Redwoods State Park in January of 2021 and visited the Old Tree Trail, which featured a 1,200-year-old redwood called “Old Tree.” Although camping is prohibited for the rest of the summer, day use areas and the backpacking trail camp will remain open. However, fires will obviously be not allowed during stark drought conditions. The park urges outdoor enthusiast to educate themselves in water conservation techniques at www.SaveOurWater.com. The route from Praça do Comércio, or Commerce Square, goes slightly uphill on its way to Park Eduardo VII, so we start our venture at the top at the park for an easy point A-B-C walk. Parque Eduardo VII is 64 acres and just north of Avenida da Liberdad. The park is named after King Edward VII of Great Britain after he visited Portugal in 1903 to strengthen the relationship between the two countries The trail goes down Avenida da Liberdad, which has several monuments like this one to Antonio Feliciano De Castillo, a famous writer from the 1800s. After Avenida da Liberdad is Monumento aos Restauradores. The path leads to Estátua do Rei Dom Pedro IV. One of the most visited locations in Lisbon is Commerce Square with its large monument to King Jose I. We go abroad to Lisbon, Portugal, starting at Parque Eduardo VII. and reaffirm their alliance. The park has a central strip of grass and an intricate hedge work, flanked by long walkways to the left and right. At the observation deck at the top of the park, you can see a statue of Marquês de Pombal and the Tagus River off in the distance. Praça do Marquês de Pombal is a roundabout and square dedicated to the Portuguese statesman and diplomat who effectively ruled the Portuguese Empire from 1750 to 1777 as chief minister to King Joseph I. From there, you venture down Avenida da Liberdade, a shaded and beautiful 1,100 meter avenue down the center of Lisbon that could draw comparisons to the Champs-Élysées in Paris. The avenue is lined with numerous monuments to several historical Portuguese figures and events. The largest monument is dedicated to the fallen soldiers in World War I. Avenida da Liberdade comes to an end at Monumento aos Restauradores (Monument to the Restorers), to memorialize Portugal’s victory in the Portuguese Restoration War of 1640-1668 and erected in 1886. The route veers slightly toward the Estátua do Rei Dom Pedro IV, another town square with two fountains and the Column of Pedro IV in between. The monument is dedicated after Pedro I, who was the first ruler of the Empire of Brazil. Before you reach the column, take a tasty detour after the Monumento aos Restauradores by turning left to A Ginjinha for a further dive into Portuguese culture. It is an historic openfront bar that opened in 1840, and where you can sip Portugal’s famous cherry liquor. The location was helped publicized by travel journalists like Anthony Staff Photos Bordain and Rick Steves. From the Column of Pedro, head down R. Augusta avenue, where you can find several gift shops and restaurants on its way to the Arco da Rau Augusta and Commerce Square. In the center of Praça do Comércio is a monument to King José I, created in 1775. Your journey ends across the street from Commerce Square at Cais das Colunas, a pier named after the two columns on the edge of the Tagus River. The location has been used as a welcoming point to several prominent figures, like Queen Elizabeth II in 1957. From there you can see Ponte 25 de April, a bridge with a striking similarity to the Golden Gate, with Santuário de Cristo Rei to its left. Take off your shoes and dip your weary feet in the water after a day of walking around Lisbon. Take a detour to A Ginjinha, a historic watering hole dating to 1840 to drink Portugal’s famous ginjinha—a cherry infused liquor. The path is nearing its end down R. Augusta avenue to the Arco da Rau Augusta. Our trail ends at Cais das Colunas, where you can take in a view of Ponte 25 de April and Santuário de Cristo Rei to its left.

articles.text: Festival. The very word connotes joy. And that’s as it should be. In the good old days, the concert season went from autumn through spring. The summer months were reserved for rest, reflection and preparing for the following concert season. As a side note, you might be interested to know that the great violinist Jascha Heifetz was afraid of the fast pace. He urged a retard in musical activities, but that did not happen. In fact, the concert season intensified. Some music festivals are famous throughout the world. The Hollywood Bowl hosts “Concerts Under the Stars.” The summer home of the New York Philharmonic was Lewisohn stadium in the heart of Harlem. During the summer of 1964 I heard some of the most illustrious musicians in the world perform there, including Marian Anderson. The festival of Two Worlds united the continents of America and Europe. It takes a tremendous backing to produce a successful festival, requiring lots of money and great organization. Remarkably, Piedmont, as small as it is, can boast a world-class music festival. Two weeks ago the non-profit Center for the Arts hosted its Fifth Annual Piedmont Chamber Music Festival, the only one of its kind in the East Bay. Modeled loosely after the Carmel Bach Festival, the visiting musicians are housed for one week by Piedmont families. The founders of the Piedmont festival are well-known to Piedmont music lovers, Piedmont native, violinist Wayne Lee and his pianist wife Juliana Han. Their organizational skills are truly awe inspiring. The programming for the festival’s three concerts was interesting in every aspect. Musicians were selected with great care and the performances proceeded like clockwork. There was an ideal balance of musical styles with every piece complementing the others. Some pieces stood out in a way which made them special. In the third concert there were three spicy Rags for string quartet written by the William Bolcom. These works were just as good as those by the more famous ragtime composer Scott Joplin. Another impressive performance was the String Quintet No. 2 by Felix Mendelsohn. The ensemble featured Francisco Fullana and Jasmine Lin on violins, Teng Li and Paul Laraia on viola, and Clancy Newman on cello. Their playing was totally resplendent and truly virtuoso. In the adagio movement, in particular, emotion welled up from the very soul of the composer. It was the very essence of the Mendelssohn ethos. The ensemble showed every evidence of marvelous technical ability. But sometimes the musicians strayed from pure musical intent and tried to show the audience they were having fun. The enthusiastic audience loved this foolishness and applauded wildly. The important thing to know is that the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival has been and continues to be a fabulous success. I remember dress rehearsals open to the public at the Hollywood Bowl. Hundreds of people came to watch early during the day and then attended the evening concerts. The concerts were every Tuesday and Thursday for the entire summer. The experience was memorable. Keep up your good work Wayne and Juliana, and if possible, add more concerts in the future. Joseph Gold is a violinist and a weekly contributor in the Post with his column, The Musical Gourmet. Musicians celebrate at the conclusion of the weeklong Piedmont Chamber Music Festival on July 24: Wayne Lee (left), Paul Laraia, Clancy Newman, Francisco Fullana, Juliana Han, Ting Li, Jasmine Lin, and Deborah Pae.

articles.text: Jeffrey LaDeur, a San Francisco-based concert pianist, is founder and artistic director of the San Francisco Piano Festival. The San Francisco International Piano Festival returns on August 18 for its fifth season, with a with a celebration of J.S. Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier. The festival continues with concerts through August 28. “In the midst of much turbulence and tragedy in our world, we continue to make music and celebrate the unstoppable force that is the creative spirit,” said festival founder and artistic director, Jeffrey LaDeur, a San Francisco-based concert pianist and one of the festival’s artists. “The 300th anniversary of Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier provides a natural focus that the festival will explore in both conventional and unexpected performances.” Festival concerts will take place in five San Francisco and Berkeley venues and will feature eight pianists and 18 composers, ranging from Bach to contemporary. articles.text: Tom Cruise and Cameron Diaz star in Knight and Day. Review by Chris Honoré Tom Cruise is, indisputably, a top-tier movie star and has been since he slid across the hardwood floor of his parents’ two-story colonial wearing white briefs, playing air guitar, in the memorable and breakthrough film, Risky Business. He lives a life that can only be imagined, one that has generated a cottage industry of fans, paparazzi and tabloid media, all desperate for information about him, professionally and most certainly personally. Cruise has always been intelligent about his career and discrete about his personal life, that is until his ill-fated interview with Oprah Winfrey. Filled with raw, adolescent emotion, in the throes of a new romance with Katie Holmes, a Hollywood ingénue with a short resume, Tom approached Oprah’s faux living room ready to levitate. He was (not to get too SoCal about it) “stoked.” So much so that Oprah barely had time enough to ask him even a preliminary question when Tom, in a moment of startling and unexpected exuberance, in front of the studio audience and millions of viewers, “jumped the couch.” It was a move that would have made any gymnast proud. As quickly as one can say Internet, “jumping the couch” dropped into the daily lexicon of common language, linked forever to that one moment when Cruise took flight and got all jiggy with it. This is all to say that Cruise has spent the ensuing post-couch years trying to dispel that YouTube, viral video moment – compounded before and after by endless displays of PDA – hoping folks would refocus on his career as an actor of seriousness and heft. The film Valkyrie, however, didn’t help. Somehow, Cruise in Nazi costume and eye patch and Sieg Heil, knee-high, heel-clicking leather boots with jodhpurs required more suspension of disbelief than most audiences were capable of. The suspicion began to take hold that Cruise was content to do Cruise, no matter the role. Which brings us to Cruise’s romantic comedy, Knight and Day, made in 2010 in which he portrays a rogue government agent, Roy Miller, in concert with Cameron Diaz as June Havens, an unsuspecting, hapless traveler on her way from Wichita to Boston. Strangely, interestingly, she’s carrying a suitcase filled with retro parts for a muscle car restoration. Accidentally she bumps into Roy in the Wichita Airport, or so she assumes. And suddenly she finds herself ensnared and in some serious jeopardy. Bad people are trying to kill Roy. Even good people are trying to kill Roy. And June is trying to keep her head down when she’s not rendered unconscious, a recurring event that’s actually charming. So, is the film good entertainment? Surprisingly, it is. What could have been a cynical attempt to package two attractive movie stars in a silly nonstarter turns out to be an enjoyable, breezy, sincere film. And, as a bonus, it has a wonderful MacGuffin. A MacGuffin is an object (papers, brief case, necklace) that soon catches the audience’s attention and helps drive the plot as a recurring theme throughout the movie. In the Maltese Falcon it was, well, the Maltese Falcon. In Knight and Day it’s the Zephyr, a selfcharging battery that provides an endless source of energy. The good guys and the bad guys are not only after the MacGuffin, but the scientist who invented it, one Simon Fleck, played geekily to the max by Paul Dano. And so the romantic thriller unfolds with Roy and June slipping into and out of improbable but nicely executed scrapes, pumping up the volume and the bullets and generally having a good time. As does the audience. Knight and Day. Directed by James Mangold, Starring Tom Cruise, Cameron Diaz, Peter Sarsgaard, and Viola Davis. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2010. Now streaming on Prime/Paramont+/Apple tv.

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Don’t worry kids, if you watched the first Ice Age and thought Scrat (Chris Wedge), the squirrel-rat, was one of the most delightful characters, you’ll be happy to know that he is back in Ice Age 2: The Meltdown. And joining him are Manfred the wooly mammoth (Ray Romano) and Sid the sloth (John Leguizamo). Soon after their journey north begins, the two are joined by Diego, the saber-toothed tiger (Denis Leary), creating a dynamic trio. The two amigos, Sid and Many, live in a valley surrounded by massive high ice walls on all sides. To their surprise, they discover that the walls are holding back a huge reservoir of water that could flood the valley. To their horror, they observe a huge chunk of the ice wall break off (climate warming), causing them to decide it’s time to leave. While all of the denizens of the valley agree that it’s time to get out of Dodge, they head south. Manny and Sid, however, go north. And thus begins their adventure. On their journey they encounter a bevy of different animals to include Ellie (Queen Latifah), a large female wooly mammoth who Manny finds attractive. They also meet up with two annoying opossums, Crash and Eddie (Sean William Scott and Jonathan Peck). Meanwhile, Sid is kidnapped by a tribe of minisloths who believe he is god-like and plan on throwing him into the mouth of a volcano. Of course, Sid manages to escape. The northern most part of the valley is flooded as the ice walls collapse, lots of close calls ensue, but in the nick of time the gang finds a large boat and make their way out of the valley to safety. Kids will enjoy the intermittent appearances of Scrat, the big-eyed rodent who is still chasing that acorn. Plus the group is in a race to escape the flooding waters from the reservoir. Can they make it? The dialogue is often hilarious, the animation top notch, and the characters fun to spend time with. Ice Age 2: The Meltdown. Animated comedy-adventure. Directed by Carlos Saldanha. With voices of Carlos Saldanha, Chris Wedge, Ray Romano, John Leguizamo. 1 hr., 31 min. Rated PG. Released in theaters in 2006. Now streaming on Disney+/ VUDU/Hulu.

articles.text: Who could have guessed where Arthur ended up? You have to love those medieval movies where everyone has a membership to 24 Hour Fitness and superb dental care. Nevertheless, King Arthur: Legend of the Sword, is an origin story regarding the Arthurian legend, that durable British myth where Arthur pulls a sword, the Excalibur, from the stone, thereby establishing his identity as the heir to the throne. That would be the throne stolen by Vortigen (Jude Law), thuggish brother of the king, Uther Pendragon (Eric Bana). Pendragon’s small son, Arthur (Charlie Hunnan), is rescued from the dark castle. His life is in danger and they put him in a small skiff. He sails into the arms of a group of big-hearted prostitutes whom having no idea who he is, raise him in their London brothel. Unaware that he is the heir to the throne, Arthur grows up on the mean streets, learning to hustle while hanging out with half a motley group. That’s sort of the story – well, it’s the beginning. The rest is seriously confusing. Some parts are mixed with sorcery and weird creatures and endless battles between Arthur and crew and Vortigen’s armies. There are brief scenes of exposition that seem more contemporary than not. This movie is a long way from Camelot and Guinevere and Lancelot. There is a Round Table that needs work and knights soon to be knighted. Gamers will love this movie. My bet is that it will morph into a franchise (despite the box office). So, if you loved this movie, no worries. Who needs a story when you have spectacle? King Arthur: Legend of the Sword. Directed by Guy Ritchie. Starring Charlie Hunnan, Eric Bana and Astrid Berges-Frisbey. 2 hrs,, 6 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2017. Now streaming on Prime/VUDU/Apple tv. Charlie Hunnan portrays King Arthur in Guy Ritchie’s King Arthur: Legend of the Sword.

He was (not to get too SoCal about it) “stoked.” So much so that Oprah barely had time enough to ask him even a preliminary question when Tom, in a moment of startling and unexpected exuberance, in front of the studio audience and millions of viewers, “jumped the couch.” It was a move that would have made any gymnast proud. As quickly as one can say Internet, “jumping the couch” dropped into the daily lexicon of common language, linked forever to that one moment when Cruise took flight and got all jiggy with it. This is all to say that Cruise has spent the ensuing post-couch years trying to dispel that YouTube, viral video moment – compounded before and after by endless displays of PDA – hoping folks would refocus on his career as an actor of seriousness and heft. The film Valkyrie, however, didn’t help. Somehow, Cruise in Nazi costume and eye patch and Sieg Heil, knee-high, heel-clicking leather boots with jodhpurs required more suspension of disbelief than most audiences were capable of. The suspicion began to take hold that Cruise was content to do Cruise, no matter the role. Which brings us to Cruise’s romantic comedy, Knight and Day, made in 2010 in which he portrays a rogue government agent, Roy Miller, in concert with Cameron Diaz as June Havens, an unsuspecting, hapless traveler on her way from Wichita to Boston. Strangely, interestingly, she’s carrying a suitcase filled with retro parts for a muscle car restoration. Accidentally she bumps into Roy in the Wichita Airport, or so she assumes. And suddenly she finds herself ensnared and in some serious jeopardy. Bad people are trying to kill Roy. Even good people are trying to kill Roy. And June is trying to keep her head down when she’s not rendered unconscious, a recurring event that’s actually charming. So, is the film good entertainment? Surprisingly, it is. What could have been a cynical attempt to package two attractive movie stars in a silly nonstarter turns out to be an enjoyable, breezy, sincere film. And, as a bonus, it has a wonderful MacGuffin. A MacGuffin is an object (papers, brief case, necklace) that soon catches the audience’s attention and helps drive the plot as a recurring theme throughout the movie. In the Maltese Falcon it was, well, the Maltese Falcon. In Knight and Day it’s the Zephyr, a selfcharging battery that provides an endless source of energy. The good guys and the bad guys are not only after the MacGuffin, but the scientist who invented it, one Simon Fleck, played geekily to the max by Paul Dano. And so the romantic thriller unfolds with Roy and June slipping into and out of improbable but nicely executed scrapes, pumping up the volume and the bullets and generally having a good time. As does the audience. Knight and Day. Directed by James Mangold, Starring Tom Cruise, Cameron Diaz, Peter Sarsgaard, and Viola Davis. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2010. By Chris Honoré You have to love those medieval movies where everyone has a membership to 24 Hour Fitness and superb dental care. Nevertheless, King Arthur: Legend of the Sword, is an origin story regarding the Arthurian legend, that durable British myth where Arthur pulls a sword, the Excalibur, from the stone, thereby establishing his identity as the heir to the throne. That would be the throne stolen by Vortigen (Jude Law), thuggish brother of the king, Uther Pendragon (Eric Bana). Pendragon’s small son, Arthur (Charlie Hunnan), is rescued from the dark castle. His life is in danger and they put him in a small skiff. He sails into the arms of a group of big-hearted prostitutes whom having no idea who he is, raise him in their London brothel. Unaware that he is the heir to the throne, Arthur grows up on the mean streets, learning to hustle while hanging out with half a motley group. That’s sort of the story – well, it’s the beginning. The rest is seriously confusing. Some parts are mixed with sorcery and weird creatures and endless battles between Arthur and crew and Vortigen’s armies. There are brief scenes of exposition that seem more contemporary than not. This movie is a long way from Camelot and Guinevere and Lancelot. There is a Round Table that needs work and knights soon to be knighted. Gamers will love this movie. My bet is that it will morph into a franchise (despite the box office). articles.text: Just the Way I Like It A bus took us from Herning, Denmark, to Hamburg, Germany for the second leg of our international choir tour this summer. The AC worked this time, so the temperature was much more amenable for exchanging our Danish homestay experiences, singing, and other choir tomfoolery. After checking into our hotel in the center of Hamburg and changing into our uniform, we immediately went to rehearsal for a concert. Our rehearsals consisted of two hours to get used to the space and run through all of our pieces and make sure we sounded our best. Our first concert in Germany was in the heart of Hamburg in a small but echoey church. The concert started with a performance by the Hamburg Girls Choir, and then us, the Ensemble group in Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. We sang No Time, a farewell song; Every Time I Feel the Spirit, a poem that enslaved people would sing; and Salut Printemps, by Claude Debussy about welcoming spring. At the end we joined the Hamburg Girls Choir to sing Hymn to Freedom and Guten Abend, Gut’ Nacht. During our three days in Hamburg we went on many adventures. We took a city boat tour (fun fact: there are 2,496 bridges in Hamburg because of all the canals. Because of that it is nicknamed “Venice of the North”). We visited the last Baroque style church in Germany, St. Michael’s, and listened to a beautiful organ concert. We went to a square with different food vendors for lunch. Hamburg has an abundance of great restaurants. For dinner the first night we split off into groups with our tour chaperones and were given the liberty to choose a restaurant and wear whatever regular clothes we had packed. After doing some light shopping and sightseeing, two friends and I popped into a grocery store and bought fresh strawberries – the best strawberries I have ever tasted. One morning my hotel roomies and I got up early and went to explore the city center. We walked to the lake and sat on a deck on the water where we could dangle our feet over the edge. We kept reminding ourselves how we were in awe of the fact that we were on tour. We made friends with ducks and picked flowers by the side of the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir singers in Ensemble performed their final concert of the tour in the main church in Mosbach near Hochhausen, Germany. lake and handed them to random people we saw on the street. Seeing the smiles on their faces made it all worth it. After our short stop in Hamburg, it was back on the road heading south. Our bus driver was a Czech named Vladimir. He studied Russian for 30 years, so I was glad to talk with him in the language I speak with my family. It was a long ride – nine hours – in what we expected to be a six-hour trip to Hochhausen. It’s safe to say that we all went crazy on the bus. When we took our lunch break, I saw two friends almost end their friendship over cheese, salami, and hummus. Everyone was hungry and food was scarce, so it was decided to share all the food. When we finally made it to Hochhausen, we stumbled out of the bus, happy to be at the final destination of our tour. The houses were multi-colored with brown trim all around to create that iconic German look. There was only one road which branched off into a couple of small ones leading to the further parts of the town. You could see it was a very small town, and our arrival possibly added another ten percent to the town’s population. We were greeted by the oneand-only Sue Malick, a longtime board member of the choir, a Piedmont resident, and my neighbor. Her husband’s family owns a rustic farm in Hochhausen, and the entire choir was invited to use their farm house as our headquarters. Sue is an amazing person. She accompanied us to every location we visited and told us the history and of the town and surrounding area. She and her husband John hosted a farewell potluck for us the day before we left. After we arrived, we dragged ourselves up multiple hills with our luggage to get to Sue’s house and meet our homestay families. The people of Hochhausen who came to take choir members to their homes, were as excited to welcome us as we were to be in their town. Our host, Karren, apparently got lost, so we were the last group to be picked up. How she managed to get lost in the tiny town that is Hochhausen is anyone’s guess. But she did arrive and took us to a house with a common room, a bathroom, and a 7x7-foot white box designated as our bedroom. We slept on air mattresses and had to share a pillow. But we didn’t complain; can you really complain to a person who lives with a fridge filled with condiments and beer? Plus, two stray kittens found their way into the backyard and into our room. We loved having so many choir members on our street so we could easily meet with friends and roam around town. One afternoon as a large group of us decided to explore the town, it started raining and raining hard. We marveled at the fat drops of warm water sliding down our faces, hitting the ground. We started dancing and singing in the rain until our legs almost gave out. We met up with another group of choir kids and made our way to a small playground as I filmed everything, including the moment when a friend fell off the see-saw. We eventually gathered in a circle and someone started singing “Rasputin” by Boney M. and everyone was trying to do the Slavic dance when you kick your legs out from underneath you while in a crouched position. After filming those iffy attempts, I summoned my Slavic ancestry, stepped in and showed how it was supposed to be done. It was certainly a night to remember. While in Hochhausen we visited the Mosbach farmers market, a big open market with stalls where farmers sell their own products. Typical German buildings surrounded the square. We hiked up many hills to find the town pool and cool off and then have an amazing dinner at a farm-to-table restaurant where I tried a Wienerschnitzel and my world was rocked. Hochhausen is the home of Count Dider who lives in a castle and owns the forest surrounding the town. His family has lived there for centuries, and he and his wife are friends of the Malicks. We were given a tour of his schloss and sang for him and his wife. One of the nights we also had a dinner hosted by the hunting club where we were served wild boar from the Count’s forest. We gave plenty of concerts, and the concerts in Hochhausen had a magic energy around them. articles.text: Photos by Mitch Shenker and Ed Kaplan. This project involved creating a great room space with a new kitchen and living room area combined. We added large openings in the rear wall with new large windows and doors to a newly landscaped rear yard. I grew up on the East Coast and moved to the Bay Area to start high school and then go on to earn my BA and MA in architecture. As a recent transplant, I remember my wonder and enjoyment of the beauty of the outdoors which is enhanced by the temperate climate we have. I noticed immediately how some ranch style homes took advantage of the indoor and outdoor connections in a minor way with large sliding patio doors. The Eichler home designs in many ways embodied that effort for the home to bring in natural light and create a easy flow to the outdoors, although they were an outlier in production home design. Most housing stock that exists today was built by developers who used stock plans from plan books, or they hired production design firms to develop generic designs to plop down (not a technical term) on any given site. Little effort was made to design the house to take advantage of the specific site’s characteristics and features. Additionally, if the house was designed many years These original three rooms at the back of this 1920’s house were combined with an addition to make one large space for a new kitchen and family room. ago, the layout and flow of the house may not suit the needs of today’s lifestyle. As I started architectural practice 40 years ago, one common lost opportunity I noticed was that most houses were not designed to open up to the outdoors, especially the rear garden space. Oddly, the back wall of many homes facing the rear garden is composed of more wall area than window area. In many homes, the utility spaces such as laundries and bathrooms take up too much of the rear walls of the house blocking off the house’s This project combined three spaces and adding about 5 feet to the rear of the house to create one large kitchen and family room. The laundry room was relocated, and the kitchen and family room were arranged to maximize on the window area out to the rear garden.

articles.text: • 2017 Domaine Saint Gayan Rasteau The Saint Gayan Rasteau is a beauty. Offering great ripeness in its kirsch, pepper and spring flower-like aromas and flavor, it is medium-bodied, silky, supple with fine tannin and good freshness. Drink over the next 5-7 years. Would partner well with roast chicken. Last month I had the opportunity to attend a seminar and tasting focused on the wines of Rasteau. The village of Rasteau is situated in the Cotes du Rhone region in the southern Rhone River area of France. It was founded by the Romans over 2000 years ago and has been continuously occupied. Still, today’s population is only 803 people. The Rasteau wine area was established in 2010 as a recognized AOC by the French government. It consists of 19,000 hectares, roughly half the size of Berkeley. In that area there are 60 small wineries and one large Cave Cooperative. Vines were probably growing in Rasteau as early as 30 B.C., but the vineyards remained largely forgotten until the Middle Ages. At that time, interest in winegrowing was revived by the ecclesiastical communities. The Rasteau vineyards were the largest in the Vaucluse. Rasteau was originally known for the production of Vines Doux Naturels – naturally sweet wines. In 1966 Rasteau dry red wines became part of the Cotes du Rhone Villages appellation, before being awarded standalone Cote du Rhone status in 2010. If you are a fan of the wines of Chateauneuf du Pape, I encourage you to sample the wines of Rasteau. They are made from the same grapes (Grenache, Syrah, Mourvedre etc.), grown in the same geographic area – the Southern Rhone Valley, and are about half the price of CDP. The following wines were four of the best of the Rasteau tasting I attended, but there are plenty of other worthy producers. cases flamboyant notes of ripe cherry fruit, along with peach and floral notes. It is framed by chewy but ripe tannins that turn silkier on the finish. Elegant and satisfying. • 2019 Lavau Rasteau A blend of 50% Syrah and 50% Grenache this was my favorite wine of the tasting. Blackberries and blueberries mingle with earth and leather on the nose. It is rich, full-bodied, concentrated and richly tannic. I would drink this big boy with a rich beef daube or cassoulet. • 2018 Domaine des Girasols Rasteau The full-bodied Girasols Rasteau is a blend of 80% Grenache and 20% Mourvedre. Black cherries, raspberries and apricots are all found in this blend of Grenache Syrah and Mourvedre. Ripe and rich, it lingers with a surprising degree of elegance on the long finish.

The village of Rasteau is situated in the Cotes du Rhone region in the southern Rhone River area of France. It was founded by the Romans over 2000 years ago and has been continuously occupied. Still, today’s population is only 803 people. The Rasteau wine area was established in 2010 as a recognized AOC by the French government. It consists of 19,000 hectares, roughly half the size of Berkeley. In that area there are 60 small wineries and one large Cave Cooperative. Vines were probably growing in Rasteau as early as 30 B.C., but the vineyards remained largely forgotten until the Middle Ages. At that time, interest in winegrowing was revived by the ecclesiastical communities. The Rasteau vineyards were the largest in the Vaucluse. Rasteau was originally known for the production of Vines Doux Naturels – naturally sweet wines. By Ed Kaplan, AIA I grew up on the East Coast and moved to the Bay Area to start high school and then go on to earn my BA and MA in architecture. As a recent transplant, I remember my wonder and enjoyment of the beauty of the outdoors which is enhanced by the temperate climate we have. articles.text: As members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group assembled on July 27, they talked about how fortunate they are to live in this area with its wonderful climate. Dallas had had 31 days of over 100-degree weather with at least ten more 100+ days forecast, and St. Louis had nine inches of rain in 24 hours. There was a solid, summer turnout of 26 walkers and one K-9 on hand. The group welcomed Recreation Department supervisor Eva Phalen and Karina Epperlein, who will be teaching Tai Chi and who gave the walkers a Tai Chi demonstration. With their sights set on seeing Beach School, the walkers went down Magnolia Avenue past the high school, on the 300 block of El Cerrito Avenue and down Oakland Avenue to the crosswalk at Latham Street. On Greenbank, they passed t he home of former State Assembly member Audie Bock and its signature white picket fence. The home, built in 1896, is now owned by the Medhekar family and has a children’s swing in the front yard. The walkers crossed Grand Avenue and continued up Greenbank to Lake Avenue. Laura Goldman, who lives nearby, pointed out a home that has recently been transformed from a small bungalow into a much larger home. Only the front door area is the same. This section of Piedmont goes back to the city’s early days. The streets Nace, Howard, and Lake, were built around 1908. The oldest houses on Nace are the 1910 “Gibson House” at 46 Nace and the 1911 “Govan House” at 18 Nace. The giant tree in front was planted by the Gibsons in the 1920s. Walking down Howard, the walkers came to Beach School’s entrance on Lake Avenue. Drawing on research from Gail Lombardi’s Piedmont Historical Society and Meghan Bennett’s History of Piedmont website, the history of the school was shared. The history of Egbert Beach Elementary School dates to the 1906 San Francisco Earthquake. On that April 18 morning, thousands of people fled the city to the East Bay. Many decided not to return, and Piedmont grew 19 times over the course of the next year. Piedmont was incorporated as a city the following year, in September 1907. City leaders decided to build two schools to serve the community. The city’s first school, Bonita Avenue School, opened in 1911, and was later renamed Havens School after the land donor, Frank C. Havens. Bonita Avenue School quickly filled to capacity, and Lake School across town on Lake Avenue, was built in 1913. Four teachers taught 100 students in six grades. In 1918, the school was renamed the “Egbert W. Beach School” in honor of Egbert William Beach, who was the first Piedmonter killed in World War I. The rapid growth of the city from 1920 to 1930 created school housing needs that could not be met with school funds. The entire enrollment at Beach was housed then in portables. At Wildwood and Havens, approximately onethird of the students were taught in cramped, wooden school rooms that the locals called “shacks.” In 1933 Beach School was condemned as a fire trap and an earthquake menace and torn down in 1934. Beach School was replaced by two separate Works Progress Administration (WPA) projects. The main wing was built in 1936, and the auditorium/classroom wing was added in 1940. It was an entire new building of eight classrooms, kindergarten, administrative unit, library, health room and auditorium. This reconstruction was part of the FDR New Deal program’s larger effort to upgrade almost 300 schools in California. In Piedmont, the WPA built a total of 28 new earthquake-ready classrooms at Beach, Havens, Wildwood, and Piedmont High School. In the early 2000s, as part of city-wide seismic facility upgrades, Beach hosted some of the Havens students for the 2009- 10 school year while Havens was entirely rebuilt. During the following year (2010-11), Wildwood students s hared the Beach campus when their school underwent construction. In 2011-12, when Beach had its turn for renovations, the school temporarily relocated to Emeryville with school buses shuttling Piedmont students back and forth each day. In the fall of 2012, Beach School re-opened its campus. The updated facilities included two new classrooms, new playground facilities, an edible garden, and seismic upgrades. Walker Pat Keller was able to find an unlocked gate on Linda Avenue and the walkers saw the old entrance to the school, a perfect location for a group photo. The group walked through the playground past the Schoolmates building and the Linda-Beach Playfield. Then it was down Linda to Grand Avenue, and a walk up Fairview Avenue. The walkers took its lower section to a very hidden pathway that took them down to Nova and Magnolia Avenues for their climb back up the hill to the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: The Piedmont Community Band mobilized the morning of July 4 for its annual appearance in the city’s 4th of July Parade. It was the first time in two years due to COVID. The band is comprised of musicians, primarily residents, ranging from amateur to professional. Some come from as far away as Minnesota. The group was founded by Jane Reed in 1984, who has organized and managed the band throughout much of its history. Mobilizing musicians was no easy feat this year and required a lot of phone calls by Reed. The band is unique for its overqualified musicians. One year a symphony musician heard there was no one who had signed up to play the triangle for the John Phillip Sousa marches, so he volunteered to play it, marching proudly down the street with the diminutive triangular metal instrument. Piedmont resident Ken Kawaichi has served as leader of the band for 36 years dressed as “Emperor Norton” - a nod to Joshua Abraham Norton, a resident of San Francisco who proclaimed himself “Norton I., Emperor of the United States” in 1859. Resident Elaine Lindenmayer is the band’s solo majorette – who, at age 70, led the band twirling and tossing her baton in the air for her 35th year. Lindenmayer said it is a tribute to the leadership of Reed and Kawaichi and the camaraderie of the band members that so many showed up this year to play. articles.text: City on track to meeting Climate Action Plan goals A report on the 2020 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions inventory prepared by Sustainability Manager Alyssa Dykman found that there was a slight reduction in emissions compared to the previous year. Piedmont City Council received and reviewed the informational report at its most recent meeting on Monday, July 18. The report provides information on the 2020 GHG emissions inventory, which includes estimates for both community and municipal emissions. Piedmont’s GHG emissions were 33,402 metric tons of CO2e, of which 722 metric tons of CO2e are attributed to municipal activities, explained Dykman. This represents a 2.3% reduction below 2019 emissions. In March 2018, City Council adopted the Piedmont Climate Action Plan 2.0, which includes the goal of reducing GHG emissions 40% below 2005 levels by 2030, and 80% below 2005 levels by 2050. According to the report, Piedmont has reduced GHG emissions 32% relative to the 2005 baseline, putting the city on track to reach its goal by 2030. “The sectors that contributed most to Piedmont’s in-territory community GHG emissions were transportation and mobile sources, contributing 50% of emissions. Residential energy [consumption] contributed 46% of total emissions,” Dykman explained. “This is the second consecutive year transportation emissions are the primary source of Piedmont’s total community emissions as a result of reductions in other sectors – particularly residential energy emissions – over the last couple of years.” Dykman explained to City Council members that actions considered to be “low-hanging fruit” have already been taken. “Further action is needed in order for the city to be on track to meet its CAP 2.0 goals,” she said. “While municipal activities in 2020 resulted in 2.2% of Piedmont’s total in-territory emissions, the City has opportunities to demonstrate leadership and commitment to reducing GHG emissions through implementing energy efficiency and electrification efforts in municipal facilities and operations.” The efforts would include investing in electric city-owned vehicles, promoting working-fromhome when possible, and maintaining a daily system to report mileage could aid in lowering employee emissions, she added. 3820 Broadway, Oakland Owners: Leah and Benjamin Bloom Piedmont High Class of ‘03

Piedmont resident Ken Kawaichi has served as leader of the band for 36 years dressed as “Emperor Norton” - a nod to Joshua Abraham Norton, a resident of San Francisco who proclaimed himself “Norton I., Emperor of the United States” in 1859. Piedmont City Council received and reviewed the informational report at its most recent meeting on Monday, July 18. The report provides information on the 2020 GHG emissions inventory, which includes estimates for both community and municipal emissions. Piedmont’s GHG emissions were 33,402 metric tons of CO2e, of which 722 metric tons of CO2e are attributed to municipal activities, explained Dykman. This represents a 2.3% reduction below 2019 emissions. In March 2018, City Council adopted the Piedmont Climate Action Plan 2.0, which includes the goal of reducing GHG emissions 40% below 2005 levels by 2030, and 80% below 2005 levels by 2050. According to the report, Piedmont has reduced GHG emissions 32% relative to the 2005 baseline, putting the city on track to reach its goal by 2030. “The sectors that contributed most to Piedmont’s in-territory community GHG emissions were transportation and mobile sources, contributing 50% of emissions. Residential energy [consumption] contributed 46% of total emissions,” Dykman explained. “This is the second consecutive year transportation emissions are the primary source of Piedmont’s total community emissions as a result of reductions in other sectors – particularly residential energy emissions – over the last couple of years.” Dykman explained to City Council members that actions considered to be “low-hanging fruit” have already been taken. “Further action is needed in order for the city to be on track to meet its CAP 2.0 goals,” she said. “While municipal activities in 2020 resulted in 2.2% of Piedmont’s total in-territory emissions, the City has opportunities to demonstrate leadership and commitment to reducing GHG emissions through implementing energy efficiency and electrification efforts in municipal facilities and operations.” The efforts would include investing in electric city-owned vehicles, promoting working-fromhome when possible, and maintaining a daily system to report mileage could aid in lowering employee emissions, she added.
